title: Friendship Filters
html:
Most of us want to be liked.

Fair enough.

Strong interpersonal connections are foundational for human flourishing, but we can’t cultivate them if we’re universally disliked. So, we cultivate a polite, cordial, and often uninteresting image of ourselves to keep us from being ostracized. If we aren’t immediately written off as a (insert your favorite pejorative here), we can sow the seeds of a healthy relationship. It’s within the context of these relationships that we’re encouraged to express the most genuine versions of ourselves.

But what happens when we maximize the number of connections we have rather than the strength of each connection? What happens when we optimize for likeability?

What we say and do becomes so far removed from how we feel that we end up being liked for something we’re not. People don’t know “us” — they know the hyper-curated interfaces of us that boast our names and faces. We pour energy into deception at the cost of nourishing meaningful relationships. At the extremes, we become liked by all, but loved by none.

However, we can counter this slide into shallowness by embracing our strangeness and making it outwardly visible, creating what I shall henceforth meme as a Friendship Filter™.

Friendship Filters can be a goofy shirt or a fun pair of earrings. A quirky hat, a funny profile picture, a unique haircut, etc. It need only filter out the judgemental from the curious. I don’t have time for people who aren’t interested in learning why I have Crocs with plastic toes sticking out of them (it’s a wild backstory!). These are not my people, so I filter them out like first-pass metabolism without giving them an ounce more of my attention than they’re worth.1

The power of friendship filters is that, if we’re brave enough to wear a bit of our funkiness on our sleeves, literally or figuratively, we selectively attract those who think spice is nice while repelling the judgy curmudgeons who would only ever call us weird.

We shouldn’t hide our uniqueness and only express what falls within a standard deviation of “normal.” That’d make the world so boring.

Let the judgy be judgy. Have fun anyway.

1

Thanks to some feedback from a friend, I realize that the wording here is a bit harsh. Judgy curmudgeons are still just people, and treating everyone with kindness should be the default. The idea that I failed to get across here is that going out of your way to be friendly to curmudgeons is a waste of energy. This is not to say that we should be cold, hostile, or dismissive towards anyone. It is only to say that we should protect our time and attention, and focus it on those closest to us.
